quizName: DMV Practice Test #14 25 Questions • Passing Score 20

questions.question: How many paths of travel are available in each traffic lane for a motorcyclist?
questions.explanation: Each traffic lane has three paths: left, center, and right.

questions.question: What is the proper footwear for riding a motorcycle?
questions.explanation: Wear sturdy shoes that cover your ankles. Short heels are best because tall heels can catch on surfaces. Tuck in any loose laces so they don't get caught.

questions.question: What does this hand signal mean?
questions.explanation: When the left arm is bent at the elbow and points downward, it means the rider will slow down or stop.

questions.question: When crossing angled railroad tracks, what is the safest approach?

options.text: Go straight ahead in your lane

questions.correctAnswerText: Go straight ahead in your lane
questions.explanation: Go straight in your lane when crossing angled tracks. Turning to approach at a right angle can be dangerous and may push you into another lane.

questions.question: How should a motorcycle be parked next to a curb?

options.text: At a 90-degree angle with the rear wheel touching the curb
At a 45-degree angle with the front tire touching the curb
Like a car, with both wheels the same distance from the curb
At the left edge of the space so drivers can see it better

questions.correctAnswerText: At a 90-degree angle with the rear wheel touching the curb
questions.explanation: Park at a 90-degree angle to the curb with your rear wheel touching it.

questions.question: How do you achieve maximum straight-line braking?

options.text: Use the front brake first, then the rear brake
Use the rear brake first, then the front brake
Use both brakes at the same time without locking either wheel
Use both brakes at the same time while locking the rear wheel

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both brakes at the same time without locking either wheel
questions.explanation: Apply both the front and rear brakes together without locking either wheel.

questions.question: If road conditions require longer stopping distance, what should you do?
questions.explanation: Increase your following distance when stopping takes longer. On slippery pavement, when you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or in heavy traffic, use at least a three-second following distance.

questions.question: What can you do to be more visible at an intersection?

options.text: Try to make eye contact with other drivers

questions.explanation: Keep your headlight on and ride in a position where oncoming traffic can see you. Keep a space cushion to allow evasive action. Never assume another driver sees you.

questions.question: When should a passenger get on a motorcycle?

options.text: As far back on the seat as possible

questions.explanation: Board after the engine starts and the transmission is in neutral. Sit as far forward as possible without blocking the rider's control. Hold onto the rider's waist, hips, or belt.

questions.question: When preparing to pass another vehicle on the left, where should you ride in your lane?
questions.explanation: Ride in the left portion of the lane to see ahead better and make yourself more visible to oncoming traffic.

questions.question: When your motorcycle's weight moves forward while braking, what can you do?

options.text: Use less pressure on the front brake.

questions.explanation: When your weight shifts forward while braking, your front wheel has more traction. This means you can press the front brake harder.

questions.question: What should you do to reduce your reaction time?
questions.explanation: In dangerous areas like intersections, keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes. This lets you react faster to hazards.

questions.question: When looking through a turn, what should you turn?
questions.explanation: Look through the turn to see where you want to go. Turn only your head, not your shoulders. Keep your eyes level.

questions.question: Where should inexperienced riders position themselves in a group?

options.text: At the back of the group.

questions.explanation: Less experienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This lets experienced riders watch and help them.

questions.question: Which of these should you NOT do to prevent fatigue on a long ride?

options.text: Limit the distance you travel each day.

questions.explanation: To stay safe, dress for bad weather, limit riding to about six hours a day, and take a break every two hours. Do not use artificial stimulants. You will crash from fatigue when they wear off.

questions.question: What formation should you use when riding in curves, turning, or entering a highway?
questions.explanation: Use single-file formation when riding through curves, making turns, and entering or leaving highways. This is safer than other formations in these situations.

questions.question: When is it most important to flash your brake light?

options.text: When you will slow down suddenly.
When there is a stop sign ahead.

questions.correctAnswerText: When you will slow down suddenly.
questions.explanation: Flash your brake light before slowing suddenly. A following driver may not see hazards ahead. Warning them gives them time to react.

questions.question: When braking on a slippery surface, what should you do?

options.text: Do not brake, but downshift instead.

questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, slow down and avoid sudden movements. Use both brakes if you need to stop.

questions.question: Which is NOT a benefit of riding in a close group?

options.text: It uses less space on the highway.
The group is easy to see.
The group is less likely to split up.
Riders reach their destination faster in a close group than a spread-out group.

questions.correctAnswerText: Riders reach their destination faster in a close group than a spread-out group.
questions.explanation: Close group riding saves space, is more visible, and keeps the group together. However, it does not make riders arrive faster than a spread-out group.

questions.question: What helps you ride safely on slippery surfaces?
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, slow down and use both brakes. Avoid sudden movements. Avoid the center of the lane and follow tire tracks left by cars. Watch for oil spots and loose gravel.

questions.question: Where do most motorcycle crashes happen?

options.text: After riding for a long time.

questions.explanation: Most motorcycle crashes happen on short trips under five miles long at speeds below 30 miles per hour.

questions.question: Where should inexperienced riders be placed in a group?

options.text: In the front of the group.
At the back of the group.

questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the lead rider. This lets experienced riders watch them from behind.

questions.question: Which is a poor reason to sound your horn?

options.text: A driver next to you is too close to the vehicle ahead of them.
A parked car has a person in the driver's seat.
You want people to look at your motorcycle.
You are passing someone who is in the street.

questions.correctAnswerText: You want people to look at your motorcycle.
questions.explanation: Use your horn to warn vehicles or pedestrians that may move into your path. Sound it when passing a driver in an adjacent lane who may cut in front of you, when a person is in a parked car, or when you see a pedestrian or bicyclist in the street. Do not use your horn just to get attention.

questions.question: How should you swerve on a motorcycle?

options.text: Press the handgrip in the direction of the turn.
Press the handgrip in the opposite direction of the turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handgrip in the direction of the turn.
questions.explanation: To swerve, press the handgrip on the side you want to turn. To swerve left, press the left handgrip, then the right to straighten. To swerve right, press the right handgrip, then the left.

questions.question: How should you look through a turn?

options.text: Turn both your head and your shoulders to get a better look.
Turn just your head, not your shoulders.
Only move your eyes, not your head.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn just your head, not your shoulders.
questions.explanation: When turning, look through the turn toward where you want to go. Turn only your head, not your shoulders. Keep your eyes level with the horizon.
